evaluated.name: AccrualIssuanceRankProduct
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual-inflated earnings are most misleading when the firm is simultaneously tapping external capital markets, because outside funding both enables the balance-sheet build and gives managers incentive to inflate reported earnings before pricing the issue.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative rank form activates the accrual penalty only among net issuers and mutes it for self-funded, cash-generating firms, so the extreme long-short buckets are populated by pure "accrual-financed" cases rather than by high-accrual firms in general. Both channels are scaled by assets and ranked cross-sectionally, keeping the interaction dimensionless and robust to outliers. Higher values should forecast lower returns as accruals reverse and issuance proceeds fail to earn their cost of capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftFundingIntensity
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr))), at), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The fraction of the asset base supported by "soft" funding, meaning non-cash accrual earnings plus net external capital raised, measures how little of the firm's growth is backed by internally generated cash.
evaluated.reasoning: Summing accrual dollars and net external financing dollars before scaling by assets creates a single funding-quality ratio in which the two themes are economically commensurate (both are dollars financing the balance sheet not produced by operations). Unlike a rank composite, it preserves magnitude information, so a firm with extreme accruals and modest issuance is treated similarly to the reverse case, while cash-rich firms retiring capital sit at the bottom. High soft-funding intensity should forecast low abnormal returns.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SustainedAccrualExternalFunding
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 3), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose earnings have been accrual-heavy on average over three years and that have cumulatively absorbed large external capital over the same window are running a chronically non-self-funding business model, and this sustained state — not a single-year event — is what predicts reversal and underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the 0-5 integer count with a continuous three-year mean accrual ratio and a three-year cumulative financing flow scaled by current assets eliminates the tie-heavy coarse sort while preserving the persistence idea, and a three-year window keeps coverage far higher than five years. The rank product still switches the accrual penalty on only for firms that actually consumed outside capital, so the extreme buckets are large and continuously populated rather than defined by a rare joint event.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnstableAccrualsRisingLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Volatile, hard-to-verify accruals signal low earnings quality, and this becomes value-destroying specifically when the firm is simultaneously levering up: creditors are funding a balance sheet whose reported profitability cannot be trusted, creating genuine financial pressure rather than mere accounting noise.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the equal-weight composite of two known first-moment predictors and instead interacts a second-moment accrual-quality measure with the change in the debt-to-assets ratio, so neither leg is a standard accrual-level or asset-growth signal. The conditional rank-product form means stable-accrual deleveraging firms and noisy-accrual firms with flat leverage both score low, isolating the specific "opaque earnings plus creditor-funded expansion" state that carries default and reversal risk.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithoutPayoutCertification
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash distributions certify that reported profits are real; therefore the accrual penalty should be concentrated in firms that pay out nothing, and should be largely switched off for firms with high accruals that are nonetheless returning substantial cash to shareholders.
evaluated.reasoning: The additive rank difference has been replaced by a multiplicative form in which the accrual rank is amplified by the rank of negative payout intensity, so the formula now literally implements the stated conditioning: high accruals plus zero payout scores near the maximum, while high accruals plus large dividends and buybacks scores near zero. Using gross distributions rather than net issuance flows makes the certification channel (commitment to pay cash) economically distinct from a net external-financing measure, and COALESCE to zero is the correct convention because a non-reported payout means no payout.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalBloatEquityFunded
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Receivable and inventory build net of operating payables that is paid for with net new equity capital combines the two classic overvaluation symptoms: soft, reversible operating assets on the balance sheet and managers willing to sell shares at current prices to fund them.
evaluated.reasoning: The contaminated share-count growth leg is replaced by net equity issuance in dollars from the cash-flow statement (sstk minus prstkc, scaled by assets), which is immune to splits and stock dividends and measures actual capital raised rather than mechanical share-count changes. The balance-sheet working-capital accrual construction is retained because it captures channel-stuffing and inventory bloat more sharply than aggregate accruals, and the rank product keeps the penalty confined to firms that genuinely financed that bloat externally rather than from operating cash.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CleanSurplusFundedWCBloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital bloat funded by newly raised outside capital predicts poor returns; measuring that capital from the balance sheet (debt increase plus the clean-surplus residual of equity growth not explained by retained earnings) captures the same economics as cash-flow issuance data but for the full cross-section.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 winner used exactly this mechanism but its financing leg (sstk minus prstkc) restricted coverage to ~10% of firm-months, which caps portfolio t-stats regardless of effect size. Clean surplus gives net external equity as DELTA(ceq) minus (ib minus dividends), and adding the change in total debt yields net capital raised from universally reported balance-sheet items, so a similar per-observation effect should translate into a materially more reliable FF5 alpha. COALESCE(dvc,0) is justified because a non-reported dividend means no dividend was paid.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EquityTiltFinancedAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual aggressiveness is most damaging when the marginal dollar of outside capital is equity rather than debt, because equity issuance is the financing form that management times against overvaluation, whereas debt-funded accruals reflect ordinary working-capital financing that creditors monitor.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 baseline pooled equity and debt flows into one net-financing leg; this replaces the level of total financing with the equity-minus-debt tilt, so a firm issuing stock while retiring debt scores high and a debt-funded firm scores low even at identical total financing. If the effect survives or strengthens, the anomaly is an overvaluation-timing story rather than a general balance-sheet-pressure story, which sharply narrows the mechanism for later generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IssuerGatedAccrualMagnitude
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at), 1), INDICATOR(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among net external financers the accrual effect should be strong and monotone in the size of the accrual, while among self-funded firms it should be economically negligible; a hard gate plus preserved accrual magnitude therefore extracts more spread than a soft rank product.
evaluated.reasoning: The rank-product family compresses accrual magnitude into a uniform [0,1] score, so extreme accrual firms get no extra weight; this variant keeps winsorized magnitude and switches the signal off entirely for non-financers, sending them to a neutral middle bucket. Comparing it against the gen-0 rank product tells us whether the payoff comes from gating or from magnitude, which is the single most useful design lesson available at this stage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftAssetStockOnRaisedCapital
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(wcap, che), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 3), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 3), TS_SUM(SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)), 3))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accumulated stock of non-cash working capital, not just this year's flow, measures how much of the balance sheet consists of soft, reversible assets; when that stock has been built up over several years of net capital infusions rather than retained cash earnings, valuation is most exposed to write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: Gen-0 tested a flow-accrual times cumulative-flow-financing version (SustainedAccrualExternalFunding) which had the weakest Fama-MacBeth slope of the accepted set, suggesting smoothed flows blur the signal; a stock-versus-multi-year-financing formulation instead contrasts levels, which is the natural way to express balance-sheet bloat. Both legs come from balance-sheet items with three-year clean-surplus accounting for external equity, so coverage should stay well above the cash-flow-based signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AbnormalAccrualSpikeAtCapitalRaise
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings management is a timing phenomenon: what matters is not whether a firm is permanently accrual-intensive (an industry and business-model trait) but whether accruals spike above the firm's own recent norm precisely in the year it raises outside capital.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the cross-sectional accrual rank with TS_RANK against the firm's own four-year history converts the accrual leg into a firm-relative abnormality measure, which absorbs permanent industry and business-model differences far more directly than an industry rank while testing a different economic object — opportunistic timing rather than chronic accounting style. Pairing it with the clean-surplus balance-sheet financing leg (debt change plus equity growth unexplained by retained earnings) keeps the financing measure free of the sparse cash-flow-statement fields, so this addresses the coverage bottleneck instead of leaving it untouched.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BorrowedDistributionsWithSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), MUL(INDICATOR(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 0), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that keeps distributing cash to shareholders while simultaneously raising net new capital is recycling outside money into payouts; when its reported earnings are also accrual-heavy rather than cash-backed, the distribution policy is being sustained by financiers rather than by operations and is vulnerable to a cut.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version's financing leg was mechanically the negative of operating plus investing cash flow, so it double-counted the low-CFO content of the accrual leg; this version drops the change in cash entirely and builds financing from balance-sheet debt and clean-surplus external equity, which is not an accounting identity in operating cash flow. The dividend-payer indicator supplies genuine conditioning rather than an additive tilt, isolating firms whose commitment to distribute coexists with both non-cash earnings and external funding needs, while non-payers sit neutrally at zero.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BookTaxGapFinancedGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(txp, 0), 1), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accruals that are not accompanied by a rise in taxes payable are the ones least likely to reflect real economic income, because managers inflate book income without incurring a cash tax obligation; such earnings become actively misleading when the firm is also raising outside capital against them.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal has used the same undifferentiated accrual measure, so this tests a genuinely new accounting-quality dimension — the book-tax divergence — as the accrual leg while holding the high-coverage clean-surplus financing leg constant. Treating an unreported taxes-payable balance as zero is the economically correct convention, and differencing it means the leg measures the change in tax obligation rather than a level that would merely proxy for profitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtCoveredDividendsSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The clearest evidence of financing strain is the dollar overlap between new borrowing and cash distributions: a firm can only be said to be borrowing to pay dividends to the extent that both are simultaneously positive and large, and that state is most damaging when reported profits are non-cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator constructs the actual overlap between the two flows rather than assuming any dividend-paying borrower is funding its payout with debt, so firms that borrow for genuine investment or that pay dividends out of cash both score near zero and stay in the neutral middle of the sort. This is a sharper and more literal formalization of the gen-1 breakout's economics using only broadly reported balance-sheet and dividend items, so coverage should exceed the cash-flow-issuance family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FinancingTurnWithSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The market underreacts to the transition into external dependence more than to its level: a firm that swings from self-funding or capital return toward net capital raising, in the same year its earnings become accrual-heavy, is revealing a newly emerged cash shortfall that has not yet been priced.
evaluated.reasoning: Every financing leg in the archive has been a level or a multi-year cumulation, so the change in net external financing intensity tests whether the anomaly is about the state of dependence or the transition into it — a distinguishable timing question with a different implied information-diffusion story. Retaining the standard accrual leg and the balance-sheet financing construction keeps the comparison clean and coverage close to the gen-1 family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ConjunctiveBloatAndCapitalRaise
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The overvaluation state requires both conditions to hold at once — soft working-capital build *and* outside funding — so the signal should be the weaker of the two ranks: a firm cannot qualify by having extreme accruals alone or extreme financing alone.
evaluated.reasoning:
A rank product lets one extreme leg compensate for a mediocre other leg, so the short decile of the archive's best signals is partly populated by pure-accrual or pure-issuance firms; MIN enforces a strict conjunction, which should purify the extreme buckets and lift ls_talpha without any point mass or degenerate ties. This abandons the dividend-yield weighting entirely — answering the concern that the added leg was a known standalone predictor with an opposing sign — and instead tests an operator-structure question (conjunction versus product) using the two legs that have performed best in the archive.
REASONING_NOTE: full support, no zero mass, coverage equal to the clean-surplus family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PayoutStrainExternallyFunded
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(ib), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A dividend that is large relative to the firm's own earnings power is a commitment the firm cannot fund internally; when that strained commitment coexists with accrual-heavy earnings and fresh outside capital, the distribution is being financed by investors rather than by operations and is vulnerable to a cut.
evaluated.reasoning:
The previous conditioner (dvc/at minus ib/at) was dominated by negative ROA, so unprofitable non-payers loaded highest and the formula measured the profitability effect instead of payout strain; the revised leg dvc/(|ib| + dvc) is bounded in [0,1], equals zero for every non-payer regardless of profitability, and rises only when dividends are large relative to the *magnitude* of earnings. Using |ib| rather than ib also removes the sign inversion for loss-makers, so the leg now measures exactly the strain concept in the hypothesis and no longer double-counts the accrual leg's low-earnings content.
INTERACTION_TYPE_NOTE: conditional
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryFinancingShockOnBloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at), 4))
evaluated.hypothesis: Habitual external financers are correctly priced as such by investors; what is not priced is a firm that turns to the capital markets at an unusual rate *for itself* in the same year its working capital balloons, because that combination reveals a newly emerged funding gap rather than a stable business model.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the size tilt — which was mechanically a size sort and contradicted the evidence that accrual and issuance mispricing concentrates in small firms — with a firm-relative financing shock measured by TS_RANK against the firm's own four-year financing history. It is the untested mirror of AbnormalAccrualSpikeAtCapitalRaise (firm-relative accruals, strong FMB but no alpha), so evaluating it tells us which leg benefits from own-history normalization and which needs a cross-sectional level, at essentially unchanged coverage.
INTERACTION_TYPE_FINAL: conditional
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RolloverPressureSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A shift in the debt mix toward short maturities means the firm must return to lenders soon; when accrual-heavy earnings are the collateral for that refinancing, the firm faces genuine rollover risk that the market prices only when the maturity wall arrives.
evaluated.reasoning: Every financing leg tested so far measures the *quantity* of capital raised; this measures its *maturity composition*, a distinct balance-sheet-pressure channel in which no new money need be raised at all for the firm to become fragile. It uses only widely reported debt items so coverage should be at the high end, and it discriminates the pressure story from the overvaluation story that the issuance-based legs capture.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DualSidedWorkingCapitalStrain
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Netting payables against receivables and inventory, as the standard accrual definition does, cancels two symptoms that are economically reinforcing: a firm that is simultaneously building soft assets, stretching its suppliers, and raising outside capital is drawing on every available funding source at once.
evaluated.reasoning: Standard working-capital accruals treat a payables build as a *credit* that offsets asset bloat, but stretched trade credit is itself a strain indicator, so the netted measure discards information; this decomposes the two sides and requires both to be high alongside external financing. It is a genuine re-specification of the accrual construct rather than a re-weighting, uses only balance-sheet items so coverage stays near the top of the archive, and its failure would be equally informative in confirming that netting is the correct accounting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EquityRaisedToPayDividends
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Selling equity while simultaneously paying dividends is the most economically indefensible round trip a firm can execute — it is tax-inefficient, dilutive, and rational only if management believes the stock is overpriced — and it is a warning of overvaluation precisely when the earnings backing the dividend are accrual-based rather than cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's MIN-overlap construction identified borrowing-to-pay-dividends; this is the untested equity counterpart, which carries a different economic interpretation (market timing and overvaluation rather than leverage strain), so evaluating it discriminates between the two stories rather than recombining tested triples. The overlap operator keeps the leg at zero for firms that only issue or only distribute, and using the clean-surplus equity issuance rather than sstk preserves the high-coverage balance-sheet construction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PreRaiseAccrualBuildup
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(LAG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings management is forward-looking: managers inflate working-capital accruals in the fiscal year *before* they approach the capital markets so that the reported track record supporting the raise looks strong, which means the diagnostic combination is prior-year bloat followed by current-year financing.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal aligns the accrual and financing legs contemporaneously, so none can distinguish accruals that *precede* a raise (window dressing, followed by reversal after the money is in) from accruals that merely accompany it (mechanical growth financing). Lagging only the accrual leg tests that sequencing directly, and because the reversal of a t−1 accrual is still ahead of the t+1 return window, the mispricing should be at least as strong as in the contemporaneous specification while using the same high-coverage balance-sheet items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueRecognitionAccrualsFinanced
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(NEG(ADD(recch, invch)), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all accruals are equally discretionary: receivable and inventory build are the components managers actually control through channel stuffing, lenient credit terms, and production for stock, whereas payables and tax accruals are largely mechanical, so the manipulation-prone components should carry the mispricing when the firm is also funding itself externally.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the contaminated depreciation-rate idea — which the critique correctly identified as asset-growth squared — with a decomposition that isolates the two accrual components with a genuine discretion story, using the cash-flow-statement items reported with their own sign convention (negated so that a receivable/inventory build scores high). It answers a question the archive cannot: whether the accrual leg's power comes from the discretionary operating components or from the netted aggregate, and it carries no mechanical overlap with the financing leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DollarBloatPlusRaisedCapital
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))))), at), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The dollar sum of working-capital bloat and newly raised outside capital measures, in commensurate units, how much of the balance sheet is supported by neither operating cash nor retained earnings, and the size of that amount — not merely a firm's cross-sectional rank — determines the severity of the subsequent correction.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version was algebraically defective because the ib terms cancelled, leaving no accrual content and double-counting dividends; replacing the ib−oancf accrual with the balance-sheet working-capital accrual removes both problems, since dvc now appears only once inside the clean-surplus term and no variable cancels. It is the magnitude-preserving counterpart of CleanSurplusFundedWCBloat (fmb −3.77, alpha −2.2%, coverage 0.110), so it isolates one clean design question — dollars versus ranks — on the archive's best-covered leg pair.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FullRoundTripDistributions
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The complete round trip — total outside capital taken in, overlapped against total cash handed out through both dividends and repurchases — measures how much of a firm's shareholder distribution is literally recycled financing, and that recycling is a negative signal exactly when reported profits are accrual-based rather than cash-backed.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested the debt-to-dividend overlap (alpha −1.8%) and the equity-to-dividend overlap (Sharpe −0.50, fmb −3.63) separately, but a firm can fund distributions with whichever source is cheapest, so restricting the overlap to one financing form or one payout form mismeasures the round trip and dilutes both legs. Aggregating both sides before taking the MIN should produce the sharpest version of the mechanism that generated the archive's largest alphas, while the overlap operator keeps investment-driven borrowers and self-funded payers at neutral.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NoSlackExternallyFundedAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Externally funded accruals are dangerous in proportion to how little balance-sheet slack remains: a firm with high net liabilities and no cash cushion cannot absorb an accrual reversal internally and must return to markets on worse terms, whereas an unlevered, cash-rich firm can simply ride it out.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far has been a flow (issuance, distributions, financing changes); the remaining untested dimension is the *stock* of financial capacity, which is what converts an accounting reversal into genuine financial distress. Net liabilities minus cash is a level variable and therefore persistent, which should help the Fama-MacBeth slope where the differenced maturity leg of RolloverPressure failed (fmb −0.43), while retaining the pressure interpretation that produced its portfolio alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ShortTermDebtRelianceSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A capital structure tilted toward short-maturity debt means the firm must repeatedly refinance; accrual-heavy earnings are the collateral for that refinancing, so the joint state is a standing rollover exposure rather than a one-year event.
evaluated.reasoning: RolloverPressure showed a real portfolio effect (alpha −2.3%, t −2.24) but no cross-sectional slope, which is the signature of an overly noisy differenced leg; replacing the one-year change in short-term-debt share with its persistent level within total capital should recover an FMB slope without abandoning the mechanism. This isolates exactly one design choice — level versus change on the maturity-structure leg — on a channel the critic judged genuinely distinct from every quantity-of-capital measure in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeveragedBuybackSoftEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), prstkc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt-funded share repurchases are the discretionary opposite of a dividend commitment: management chooses to lever up to buy stock, and when reported earnings supporting that decision are accrual-based, the buyback is more likely a price-supporting or EPS-managing action than a value-creating one.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has established that borrowing to pay dividends predicts poor returns, but repurchases carry the opposite prior in the literature (buybacks generally predict positive abnormal returns), so testing the debt-funded repurchase overlap is a genuine discrimination test rather than a restatement: if it is also negative, the mechanism is capital recycling per se, not dividend rigidity. The MIN overlap keeps deleveraging repurchasers and investment-driven borrowers neutral, so the extreme bucket contains only firms that visibly financed the buyback with new debt.

evaluated.name: ChronicCapitalRecycling
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0))), 3), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of funding distributions with fresh capital can be timing or transition, but a firm that recycles outside money into shareholder payouts year after year has a structural inability to fund its own distribution policy, and that chronic state is what makes accrual-based earnings genuinely unreliable.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not an operator swap on the round-trip proposal but a change in the economic object — chronic versus episodic recycling — motivated by the fact that annual overlap flows are lumpy (a single large raise or a one-off special dividend dominates), which is a plausible reason the debt-only overlap achieved only t = −1.44 despite a sound construction. Cumulating three years of the overlap before scaling smooths that lumpiness while keeping the MIN's one-sided interpretation, so both the cross-sectional slope and portfolio stability should improve relative to the one-year version.

evaluated.name: ExternallyMatchedBloatDollars
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))))), at), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is the number of dollars of working-capital build that were actually matched by newly raised outside capital — bloat financed from operating cash is self-limiting, and capital raised for genuine investment is not accrual-driven, so only the overlap of the two represents externally financed soft assets.
evaluated.reasoning: The rejected version multiplied a signed magnitude by a positive rank, which perversely made rigid-dividend self-funded firms the strongest buys; taking the MIN of the two dollar flows instead makes the construction one-sided by design — it is large and positive only when bloat and financing are jointly large, and it is negative only for firms that are simultaneously liquidating working capital and returning capital, which is exactly the intended long leg. It preserves dollar magnitude, which produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (fmb −4.01), while adding the overlap conditioning that produced the archive's largest alphas, and it uses only balance-sheet items so coverage stays at the archive maximum of about 0.110.

evaluated.name: PayoutAgainstLiquidityFunded
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(che, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A dividend is a strain not when it is large relative to reported earnings — which are themselves suspect — but when it is large relative to the cash the firm actually holds; such a payout can only be sustained by continued access to capital markets, and accrual-heavy earnings make that access fragile.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's payout-strain conditioner measured the dividend against |ib|, an accrual-contaminated denominator that partly re-expresses the accrual leg; measuring it against cash holdings instead makes the conditioner a pure liquidity-commitment ratio and connects the two mechanisms that generated the largest alphas (payout rigidity and absent financial slack). Both are bounded in [0,1] and the comparison against PayoutStrainExternallyFunded isolates whether earnings coverage or liquidity coverage is the operative form of distribution strain.

evaluated.name: AccrualQualityDriftUnderLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A multi-year drift toward accrual-based earnings is a slow deterioration in economic performance that management is smoothing over; at firms carrying net debt, that deterioration eventually collides with fixed claims, whereas cash-rich firms can absorb it indefinitely.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg tested so far is a level, a one-year change, or a firm-relative position; a fitted multi-year slope is a different statistical object that captures gradual, non-episodic erosion of earnings quality, which is precisely the kind of deterioration a leveraged capital structure cannot tolerate. Pairing the trend with the persistent net-debt state rather than a financing flow tests whether the strong alphas from state conditioners survive when the accounting leg is also a slow-moving construct, at a modest coverage cost from the four-year window.

evaluated.name: SlackErosionWithAccrualBuild
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, ADD(che, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The informative event is not the level of financial slack but its erosion: a firm whose cash position is falling relative to its debt obligations at the same time that its working capital is ballooning is converting liquid resources into soft assets, which is the transition from a comfortable balance sheet into a constrained one.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's state conditioners are all static levels (net debt, maturity mix, payer status) that produce alpha without a cross-sectional slope, plausibly because they identify firm *types* rather than deteriorating situations; a bounded change measure identifies firms moving into constraint, which should be both more monotone across the cross-section and more informative about the coming year. It abandons the rejected ensemble structure entirely and introduces a dynamic-slack channel that neither parent signal contained.

evaluated.name: ExternallyBuiltAssetBaseAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), 5), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Five years of cumulative outside capital measures what fraction of the current asset base was built with investors' money rather than retained cash; firms whose balance sheets are structurally externally financed have no demonstrated ability to self-fund, so accrual-heavy earnings today are far more likely to be an accommodation to that dependence than a temporary timing difference.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the identity-collapsing net-operating-asset construction with a conditioner that is genuinely independent of the accrual leg — a five-year accumulated financing stock rather than a contemporaneous balance-sheet difference — and it directly addresses the generation's central question by converting a flow into a persistent state without importing a leverage characteristic. Unlike the gen-0 cumulative test, the accrual leg is the current-year measure (so the interaction is "structural dependence times current aggressiveness") and the financing stock is built from balance-sheet clean surplus rather than sparse cash-flow items, preserving coverage near 0.09 despite the five-year window.

evaluated.name: SoftShareOfGrowthEquityFunded
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(ABS(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)))), ABS(DELTA(at, 1))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms can grow their balance sheets identically while one adds plant and the other adds receivables and inventory; what predicts poor returns is the *share* of growth that is soft, and that share is most suspect when the growth was funded by selling equity rather than by retained cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The flow family's alphas are plausibly absorbed by CMA because their accrual and financing legs both scale with total asset growth; expressing the accrual leg as a bounded share of total balance-sheet growth removes the size-of-growth component and leaves only its composition, which the investment factor does not span. Pairing it with clean-surplus net equity issuance keeps the overvaluation-timing interpretation while using high-coverage balance-sheet items.

evaluated.name: PeakDebtCapacityAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), TS_MAX(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt capacity is firm-specific: what matters is not how levered a firm is versus other firms but whether it has pushed leverage to the highest level it has ever sustained, because that is the point at which lenders stop accommodating and an accrual reversal can no longer be refinanced away.
evaluated.reasoning: Every leverage conditioner tested so far is a cross-sectional level, which loads on the value and profitability dimensions FF5 already prices; distance from a firm's own five-year maximum leverage is a self-normalized capacity measure that is close to zero for firms at their ceiling regardless of industry or size, so it should be far less spanned by the factor model and more comparable across firms in a pooled regression. This is a genuinely different conditioning concept — proximity to an internal constraint rather than the level of a characteristic.

evaluated.name: ContractualClaimMixAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all liabilities behave alike under stress: interest-bearing debt carries fixed dates and covenants while payables and accrued expenses flex with the business, so a firm whose obligations are predominantly contractual has far less capacity to absorb an accrual reversal than one financed by trade credit at the same total leverage.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has repeatedly tested the *amount* of leverage but never its contractual character, and this ratio is deliberately scale-free and independent of total indebtedness, so it should not merely re-proxy the value/leverage tilt that FF5 partially spans. It is built from two universally reported balance-sheet aggregates, so coverage should be at the top of the archive, and it isolates the balance-sheet-pressure channel from the overvaluation channel more cleanly than any quantity-of-financing leg.

evaluated.name: RaisedCapitalYetCashFell
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), NEG(DELTA(che, 1))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that raised outside capital and still ended the year with less cash consumed the entire raise plus part of its buffer; combined with earnings that are largely accruals, this is direct evidence that the business is burning cash faster than the capital markets are willing to replace it.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the previously rejected issuance-minus-cash-change construction, which collapsed by identity into negative operating-plus-investing cash flow; the MIN overlap is positive only when the firm both raised capital *and* depleted cash, so firms that raise and hoard, or that shrink cash while returning capital, sit at neutral rather than loading on the short leg. evaluated.name: PayoutEscalationAgainstAccrualDecay
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), at), 4)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital policy should adjust to fundamentals; when a firm raises its distribution year after year while the cash backing of its earnings deteriorates over the same years, management is either misreading its own business or deliberately signalling a strength that the accounting no longer supports, and that divergence resolves badly.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a re-normalization of the archived leverage interaction: it discards the leverage state entirely and instead pairs two fitted multi-year slopes, testing a divergence between the *direction* of accounting quality and the *direction* of payout policy — a concept no archive signal contains, since every payout leg tested has been a contemporaneous level or ratio. The trend construction is what produced the archive's largest alpha, and pairing it with an escalating commitment rather than a static balance-sheet characteristic should give the pooled cross-sectional regression a variable that is not dominated by persistent firm type.

evaluated.name: NeverCutDividendFloorAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The binding commitment is not this year's dividend but the floor the firm has never breached in four years: that floor is what management will protect by borrowing, issuing, or deferring investment, so it becomes a genuine claim on future cash precisely when reported earnings stop being cash-backed.
evaluated.reasoning: Every payout conditioner in the archive measures the current distribution relative to earnings, cash, or assets; the four-year minimum measures the *durable* portion of the commitment, which distinguishes a firm with a large sustained dividend from one that just paid a large special or recently initiated, and treats an unreported dividend as zero, which is the economically correct convention. It replaces the rejected three-leg industry neutralization with a two-leg structure that has historically preserved Fama-MacBeth slope power, while targeting the rigidity mechanism that generated the archive's largest alphas.

evaluated.name: RigidityAmplifiedAccrualMagnitude
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Claim rigidity does not create mispricing, it amplifies it symmetrically: among firms with mostly contractual obligations, aggressive accruals are punished harder and genuinely cash-backed earnings are rewarded more, because these are the firms for which the difference between paper profit and cash actually determines solvency.
evaluated.reasoning: Every rigid-claim signal in the archive compresses accruals into a rank, discarding magnitude, which is precisely what the strongest cross-sectional slopes (DollarBloat fmb −4.01, SoftFundingIntensity −3.61) retain — so this tests whether keeping signed accrual magnitude while letting rigidity scale it can deliver the FMB slope that the rank-product family loses. Unlike the gen-4 proposal rejected for symmetric amplification, the hypothesis here is explicitly two-sided and matches the constrained-firm amplification story, so the functional form and the economics agree.

evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings that generate no incremental tax obligation are the least likely to be real, and the firms least able to survive that discovery are those whose obligations are contractual rather than operating, so the two diagnostics should reinforce each other.

evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dlc, TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4)), ADD(che, ADD(dlc, TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The binding constraint is the cash the firm must produce within twelve months — debt maturing this year plus the dividend it has never cut — measured against the cash it actually holds; when those claims dominate the liquidity available and reported earnings are mostly accruals, the required cash simply is not there.

evaluated.hypothesis: Increasing the dividend is a public commitment to future cash payments; doing so in the same year the firm takes in net outside capital means the commitment is being escalated on borrowed strength, and if the earnings behind it are accrual-based the escalation is a signalling gamble rather than a statement of capacity.

evaluated.name: CapitalRaisedWhileFixedAssetsShrank
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), NEG(DELTA(SUB(at, act), 1))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm raises outside capital in a year its long-lived asset base is shrinking, the money did not fund investment — it was absorbed by the operating cycle or by losses — and that is the least productive possible use of external finance, especially when reported profit is accrual-driven.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version failed to resolve the double-count because Δche and Δdlc appeared in both legs; replacing the cash-drawdown leg with the decline in non-current assets removes every shared term with the accrual leg while preserving the "the raise was consumed, not invested" economics. evaluated.name: DebtVersusServicingResourcesAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(che, MAX(ADD(ib, dp), dp))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt should be judged against the resources available to service it — cash on hand plus a year of pre-depreciation earnings — and a firm whose obligations dwarf those resources cannot absorb an accrual reversal, because the reversal removes precisely the reported profit that the servicing capacity was assumed to contain.
evaluated.reasoning: The rejected version put oancf in both legs, making the product close to a squared low-cash-flow characteristic; this conditioner contains no oancf at all, and while ib appears in both, it enters with opposing effects (higher earnings raise the accrual leg but also raise servicing capacity, lowering the conditioner), so the interaction cannot be a same-direction double count. Bounding the ratio as debt over debt-plus-resources removes the explosive-denominator problem entirely, and flooring the earnings term at depreciation keeps the measure defined and positive for loss-making firms.

evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is the fraction of reported profit that is not backed by cash, not its size relative to assets: a firm whose entire earnings figure is accrual while its cash flow is negative is qualitatively different from an asset-heavy firm with the same accrual-to-assets ratio, and that qualitative difference is what external funding exposes.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg in this archive is deflated by assets, which makes it mechanically correlated with asset intensity and heavily outlier-driven; a bounded accrual-share-of-earnings measure in [−1, 1] is a different economic construct — earnings composition rather than balance-sheet intensity — and its boundedness should produce more monotone cross-sectional behaviour without the winsorization crutch. evaluated.hypothesis: Preferred dividends are a claim that ranks ahead of common shareholders and must be served before any residual value accrues to them; when the earnings supporting that seniority structure are accrual-based rather than cash, the common equity is the tranche that absorbs the shortfall.

evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), ABS(oancf)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, ADD(ABS(oancf), dvt)), 1)))

evaluated.reasoning: The rejected version failed because a non-negative preferred-claim level puts the large block of non-preferred firms at the bottom of the rank rather than the middle; taking the *change* in total distribution coverage fixes this structurally, since firms with no distributions have a change of exactly zero, which sits at the centre of a two-sided distribution rather than at an extreme. evaluated.name: TradeCreditReplacedByContractualDebt
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When suppliers shorten terms, the firm must replace flexible, interest-free operating credit with contractual borrowing; that substitution converts a claim that bends in bad times into one that does not, and it is initiated by the creditors who monitor the firm most closely.

evaluated.name: PayoutCoverageWithHardeningClaims
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(oancf), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A dividend that already consumes most of operating cash becomes dangerous when the firm's obligation mix is hardening — flexible operating liabilities giving way to contractual debt — because each year less of the balance sheet can absorb a cash shortfall without a covenant or a maturity forcing the issue.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique of the static debt-share conditioner is well founded — it has produced large alphas with null slopes in four separate archive signals, the signature of a persistent distress characteristic mis-loading against FF5 — so this replaces the level with its one-year change, which identifies firms whose claim structure is *becoming* rigid rather than firms that are permanently levered. Paired with the archive's strongest cross-sectional leg (payout absorption of operating cash, fmb −4.43), both components now vary within firm over time, which is the configuration that has consistently produced joint slope and alpha evidence in this run.

considered.name: AccrualIssuanceRankProduct
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual-inflated earnings are most misleading when the firm is simultaneously tapping external capital markets, because outside funding both enables the balance-sheet build and gives managers incentive to inflate reported earnings before pricing the issue.
considered.reasoning: The multiplicative rank form activates the accrual penalty only among net issuers and mutes it for self-funded, cash-generating firms, so the extreme long-short buckets are populated by pure "accrual-financed" cases rather than by high-accrual firms in general. Both channels are scaled by assets and ranked cross-sectionally, keeping the interaction dimensionless and robust to outliers. Higher values should forecast lower returns as accruals reverse and issuance proceeds fail to earn their cost of capital.

considered.name: SoftFundingIntensity
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr))), at), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The fraction of the asset base supported by "soft" funding, meaning non-cash accrual earnings plus net external capital raised, measures how little of the firm's growth is backed by internally generated cash.
considered.reasoning: Summing accrual dollars and net external financing dollars before scaling by assets creates a single funding-quality ratio in which the two themes are economically commensurate (both are dollars financing the balance sheet not produced by operations). Unlike a rank composite, it preserves magnitude information, so a firm with extreme accruals and modest issuance is treated similarly to the reverse case, while cash-rich firms retiring capital sit at the bottom. High soft-funding intensity should forecast low abnormal returns.

considered.name: SustainedAccrualExternalFunding
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 3), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose earnings have been accrual-heavy on average over three years and that have cumulatively absorbed large external capital over the same window are running a chronically non-self-funding business model, and this sustained state — not a single-year event — is what predicts reversal and underperformance.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the 0-5 integer count with a continuous three-year mean accrual ratio and a three-year cumulative financing flow scaled by current assets eliminates the tie-heavy coarse sort while preserving the persistence idea, and a three-year window keeps coverage far higher than five years. considered.name: UnstableAccrualsRisingLeverage
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Volatile, hard-to-verify accruals signal low earnings quality, and this becomes value-destroying specifically when the firm is simultaneously levering up: creditors are funding a balance sheet whose reported profitability cannot be trusted, creating genuine financial pressure rather than mere accounting noise.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the equal-weight composite of two known first-moment predictors and instead interacts a second-moment accrual-quality measure with the change in the debt-to-assets ratio, so neither leg is a standard accrual-level or asset-growth signal. The conditional rank-product form means stable-accrual deleveraging firms and noisy-accrual firms with flat leverage both score low, isolating the specific "opaque earnings plus creditor-funded expansion" state that carries default and reversal risk.

considered.name: AccrualsWithoutPayoutCertification
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Cash distributions certify that reported profits are real; therefore the accrual penalty should be concentrated in firms that pay out nothing, and should be largely switched off for firms with high accruals that are nonetheless returning substantial cash to shareholders.
considered.reasoning: The additive rank difference has been replaced by a multiplicative form in which the accrual rank is amplified by the rank of negative payout intensity, so the formula now literally implements the stated conditioning: high accruals plus zero payout scores near the maximum, while high accruals plus large dividends and buybacks scores near zero. Using gross distributions rather than net issuance flows makes the certification channel (commitment to pay cash) economically distinct from a net external-financing measure, and COALESCE to zero is the correct convention because a non-reported payout means no payout.

considered.name: WorkingCapitalBloatEquityFunded
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Receivable and inventory build net of operating payables that is paid for with net new equity capital combines the two classic overvaluation symptoms: soft, reversible operating assets on the balance sheet and managers willing to sell shares at current prices to fund them.
considered.reasoning: The contaminated share-count growth leg is replaced by net equity issuance in dollars from the cash-flow statement (sstk minus prstkc, scaled by assets), which is immune to splits and stock dividends and measures actual capital raised rather than mechanical share-count changes. considered.name: CleanSurplusFundedWCBloat
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))

considered.name: EquityTiltFinancedAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))

considered.name: IssuerGatedAccrualMagnitude
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at), 1), INDICATOR(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 0))

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(wcap, che), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 3), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 3), TS_SUM(SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)), 3))), at)))

considered.name: AbnormalAccrualSpikeAtCapitalRaise
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))

considered.name: BorrowedDistributionsWithSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), MUL(INDICATOR(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 0), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that keeps distributing cash to shareholders while simultaneously raising net new capital is recycling outside money into payouts; when its reported earnings are also accrual-heavy rather than cash-backed, the distribution policy is being sustained by financiers rather than by operations and is vulnerable to a cut.

The dividend-payer indicator supplies genuine conditioning rather than an additive tilt, isolating firms whose commitment to distribute coexists with both non-cash earnings and external funding needs, while non-payers sit neutrally at zero.

considered.name: BookTaxGapFinancedGrowth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(txp, 0), 1), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Accruals that are not accompanied by a rise in taxes payable are the ones least likely to reflect real economic income, because managers inflate book income without incurring a cash tax obligation; such earnings become actively misleading when the firm is also raising outside capital against them.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal has used the same undifferentiated accrual measure, so this tests a genuinely new accounting-quality dimension — the book-tax divergence — as the accrual leg while holding the high-coverage clean-surplus financing leg constant. Treating an unreported taxes-payable balance as zero is the economically correct convention, and differencing it means the leg measures the change in tax obligation rather than a level that would merely proxy for profitability.

considered.name: DebtCoveredDividendsSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The clearest evidence of financing strain is the dollar overlap between new borrowing and cash distributions: a firm can only be said to be borrowing to pay dividends to the extent that both are simultaneously positive and large, and that state is most damaging when reported profits are non-cash.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator constructs the actual overlap between the two flows rather than assuming any dividend-paying borrower is funding its payout with debt, so firms that borrow for genuine investment or that pay dividends out of cash both score near zero and stay in the neutral middle of the sort. This is a sharper and more literal formalization of the gen-1 breakout's economics using only broadly reported balance-sheet and dividend items, so coverage should exceed the cash-flow-issuance family.

considered.name: FinancingTurnWithSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The market underreacts to the transition into external dependence more than to its level: a firm that swings from self-funding or capital return toward net capital raising, in the same year its earnings become accrual-heavy, is revealing a newly emerged cash shortfall that has not yet been priced.
considered.reasoning: Every financing leg in the archive has been a level or a multi-year cumulation, so the change in net external financing intensity tests whether the anomaly is about the state of dependence or the transition into it — a distinguishable timing question with a different implied information-diffusion story. Retaining the standard accrual leg and the balance-sheet financing construction keeps the comparison clean and coverage close to the gen-1 family.

considered.name: ConjunctiveBloatAndCapitalRaise
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The overvaluation state requires both conditions to hold at once — soft working-capital build *and* outside funding — so the signal should be the weaker of the two ranks: a firm cannot qualify by having extreme accruals alone or extreme financing alone.
considered.reasoning:
A rank product lets one extreme leg compensate for a mediocre other leg, so the short decile of the archive's best signals is partly populated by pure-accrual or pure-issuance firms; MIN enforces a strict conjunction, which should purify the extreme buckets and lift ls_talpha without any point mass or degenerate ties. This abandons the dividend-yield weighting entirely — answering the concern that the added leg was a known standalone predictor with an opposing sign — and instead tests an operator-structure question (conjunction versus product) using the two legs that have performed best in the archive.

considered.name: PayoutStrainExternallyFunded
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(ib), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))))
considered.hypothesis: A dividend that is large relative to the firm's own earnings power is a commitment the firm cannot fund internally; when that strained commitment coexists with accrual-heavy earnings and fresh outside capital, the distribution is being financed by investors rather than by operations and is vulnerable to a cut.
considered.reasoning:
The previous conditioner (dvc/at minus ib/at) was dominated by negative ROA, so unprofitable non-payers loaded highest and the formula measured the profitability effect instead of payout strain; the revised leg dvc/(|ib| + dvc) is bounded in [0,1], equals zero for every non-payer regardless of profitability, and rises only when dividends are large relative to the *magnitude* of earnings. Using |ib| rather than ib also removes the sign inversion for loss-makers, so the leg now measures exactly the strain concept in the hypothesis and no longer double-counts the accrual leg's low-earnings content.

considered.name: OwnHistoryFinancingShockOnBloat
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at), 4))
considered.hypothesis: Habitual external financers are correctly priced as such by investors; what is not priced is a firm that turns to the capital markets at an unusual rate *for itself* in the same year its working capital balloons, because that combination reveals a newly emerged funding gap rather than a stable business model.
considered.reasoning:
This replaces the size tilt — which was mechanically a size sort and contradicted the evidence that accrual and issuance mispricing concentrates in small firms — with a firm-relative financing shock measured by TS_RANK against the firm's own four-year financing history. It is the untested mirror of AbnormalAccrualSpikeAtCapitalRaise (firm-relative accruals, strong FMB but no alpha), so evaluating it tells us which leg benefits from own-history normalization and which needs a cross-sectional level, at essentially unchanged coverage.

considered.name: RolloverPressureSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A shift in the debt mix toward short maturities means the firm must return to lenders soon; when accrual-heavy earnings are the collateral for that refinancing, the firm faces genuine rollover risk that the market prices only when the maturity wall arrives.
considered.reasoning: Every financing leg tested so far measures the *quantity* of capital raised; this measures its *maturity composition*, a distinct balance-sheet-pressure channel in which no new money need be raised at all for the firm to become fragile. It uses only widely reported debt items so coverage should be at the high end, and it discriminates the pressure story from the overvaluation story that the issuance-based legs capture.

considered.name: DualSidedWorkingCapitalStrain
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Netting payables against receivables and inventory, as the standard accrual definition does, cancels two symptoms that are economically reinforcing: a firm that is simultaneously building soft assets, stretching its suppliers, and raising outside capital is drawing on every available funding source at once.
considered.reasoning: Standard working-capital accruals treat a payables build as a *credit* that offsets asset bloat, but stretched trade credit is itself a strain indicator, so the netted measure discards information; this decomposes the two sides and requires both to be high alongside external financing. It is a genuine re-specification of the accrual construct rather than a re-weighting, uses only balance-sheet items so coverage stays near the top of the archive, and its failure would be equally informative in confirming that netting is the correct accounting.

considered.name: EquityRaisedToPayDividends
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Selling equity while simultaneously paying dividends is the most economically indefensible round trip a firm can execute — it is tax-inefficient, dilutive, and rational only if management believes the stock is overpriced — and it is a warning of overvaluation precisely when the earnings backing the dividend are accrual-based rather than cash.
considered.reasoning: The archive's MIN-overlap construction identified borrowing-to-pay-dividends; this is the untested equity counterpart, which carries a different economic interpretation (market timing and overvaluation rather than leverage strain), so evaluating it discriminates between the two stories rather than recombining tested triples. considered.name: PreRaiseAccrualBuildup
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(LAG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings management is forward-looking: managers inflate working-capital accruals in the fiscal year *before* they approach the capital markets so that the reported track record supporting the raise looks strong, which means the diagnostic combination is prior-year bloat followed by current-year financing.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal aligns the accrual and financing legs contemporaneously, so none can distinguish accruals that *precede* a raise (window dressing, followed by reversal after the money is in) from accruals that merely accompany it (mechanical growth financing). Lagging only the accrual leg tests that sequencing directly, and because the reversal of a t−1 accrual is still ahead of the t+1 return window, the mispricing should be at least as strong as in the contemporaneous specification while using the same high-coverage balance-sheet items.

considered.name: RevenueRecognitionAccrualsFinanced
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(NEG(ADD(recch, invch)), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Not all accruals are equally discretionary: receivable and inventory build are the components managers actually control through channel stuffing, lenient credit terms, and production for stock, whereas payables and tax accruals are largely mechanical, so the manipulation-prone components should carry the mispricing when the firm is also funding itself externally.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the contaminated depreciation-rate idea — which the critique correctly identified as asset-growth squared — with a decomposition that isolates the two accrual components with a genuine discretion story, using the cash-flow-statement items reported with their own sign convention (negated so that a receivable/inventory build scores high). considered.name: DollarBloatPlusRaisedCapital
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))))), at), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The dollar sum of working-capital bloat and newly raised outside capital measures, in commensurate units, how much of the balance sheet is supported by neither operating cash nor retained earnings, and the size of that amount — not merely a firm's cross-sectional rank — determines the severity of the subsequent correction.
considered.reasoning: The previous version was algebraically defective because the ib terms cancelled, leaving no accrual content and double-counting dividends; replacing the ib−oancf accrual with the balance-sheet working-capital accrual removes both problems, since dvc now appears only once inside the clean-surplus term and no variable cancels. considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The complete round trip — total outside capital taken in, overlapped against total cash handed out through both dividends and repurchases — measures how much of a firm's shareholder distribution is literally recycled financing, and that recycling is a negative signal exactly when reported profits are accrual-based rather than cash-backed.

considered.name: NoSlackExternallyFundedAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Externally funded accruals are dangerous in proportion to how little balance-sheet slack remains: a firm with high net liabilities and no cash cushion cannot absorb an accrual reversal internally and must return to markets on worse terms, whereas an unlevered, cash-rich firm can simply ride it out.
considered.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far has been a flow (issuance, distributions, financing changes); the remaining untested dimension is the *stock* of financial capacity, which is what converts an accounting reversal into genuine financial distress. Net liabilities minus cash is a level variable and therefore persistent, which should help the Fama-MacBeth slope where the differenced maturity leg of RolloverPressure failed (fmb −0.43), while retaining the pressure interpretation that produced its portfolio alpha.

considered.name: ShortTermDebtRelianceSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
considered.hypothesis: A capital structure tilted toward short-maturity debt means the firm must repeatedly refinance; accrual-heavy earnings are the collateral for that refinancing, so the joint state is a standing rollover exposure rather than a one-year event.
considered.reasoning: RolloverPressure showed a real portfolio effect (alpha −2.3%, t −2.24) but no cross-sectional slope, which is the signature of an overly noisy differenced leg; replacing the one-year change in short-term-debt share with its persistent level within total capital should recover an FMB slope without abandoning the mechanism. This isolates exactly one design choice — level versus change on the maturity-structure leg — on a channel the critic judged genuinely distinct from every quantity-of-capital measure in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeveragedBuybackSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), prstkc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Debt-funded share repurchases are the discretionary opposite of a dividend commitment: management chooses to lever up to buy stock, and when reported earnings supporting that decision are accrual-based, the buyback is more likely a price-supporting or EPS-managing action than a value-creating one.
considered.reasoning: The archive has established that borrowing to pay dividends predicts poor returns, but repurchases carry the opposite prior in the literature (buybacks generally predict positive abnormal returns), so testing the debt-funded repurchase overlap is a genuine discrimination test rather than a restatement: if it is also negative, the mechanism is capital recycling per se, not dividend rigidity. The MIN overlap keeps deleveraging repurchasers and investment-driven borrowers neutral, so the extreme bucket contains only firms that visibly financed the buyback with new debt.

considered.name: ChronicCapitalRecycling
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), ADD(COALESCE(dvc, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0))), 3), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of funding distributions with fresh capital can be timing or transition, but a firm that recycles outside money into shareholder payouts year after year has a structural inability to fund its own distribution policy, and that chronic state is what makes accrual-based earnings genuinely unreliable.
considered.reasoning: This is not an operator swap on the round-trip proposal but a change in the economic object — chronic versus episodic recycling — motivated by the fact that annual overlap flows are lumpy (a single large raise or a one-off special dividend dominates), which is a plausible reason the debt-only overlap achieved only t = −1.44 despite a sound construction. Cumulating three years of the overlap before scaling smooths that lumpiness while keeping the MIN's one-sided interpretation, so both the cross-sectional slope and portfolio stability should improve relative to the one-year version.

considered.name: ExternallyMatchedBloatDollars
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))))), at), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is the number of dollars of working-capital build that were actually matched by newly raised outside capital — bloat financed from operating cash is self-limiting, and capital raised for genuine investment is not accrual-driven, so only the overlap of the two represents externally financed soft assets.
considered.reasoning: The rejected version multiplied a signed magnitude by a positive rank, which perversely made rigid-dividend self-funded firms the strongest buys; taking the MIN of the two dollar flows instead makes the construction one-sided by design — it is large and positive only when bloat and financing are jointly large, and it is negative only for firms that are simultaneously liquidating working capital and returning capital, which is exactly the intended long leg. It preserves dollar magnitude, which produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (fmb −4.01), while adding the overlap conditioning that produced the archive's largest alphas, and it uses only balance-sheet items so coverage stays at the archive maximum of about 0.110.

considered.name: UncoveredNearTermDebtAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(che, dlc))))
considered.hypothesis: Rollover risk is not the level of short-term debt but the share of it that cash on hand cannot retire; when a firm with uncovered near-term maturities also reports earnings that are largely accruals, the cash needed to refinance is not being generated and lenders will eventually reprice.

It keeps the two-leg structure that has historically preserved FMB power and uses items reported by nearly all firms.
