considered.name: PayoutAgainstLiquidityFunded
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(che, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))))
considered.hypothesis: A dividend is a strain not when it is large relative to reported earnings — which are themselves suspect — but when it is large relative to the cash the firm actually holds; such a payout can only be sustained by continued access to capital markets, and accrual-heavy earnings make that access fragile.

considered.name: AccrualQualityDriftUnderLeverage
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
considered.hypothesis: A multi-year drift toward accrual-based earnings is a slow deterioration in economic performance that management is smoothing over; at firms carrying net debt, that deterioration eventually collides with fixed claims, whereas cash-rich firms can absorb it indefinitely.

Pairing the trend with the persistent net-debt state rather than a financing flow tests whether the strong alphas from state conditioners survive when the accounting leg is also a slow-moving construct, at a modest coverage cost from the four-year window.

considered.name: MaturityMismatchedAccrualFunding
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(DELTA(dlc, 1), DELTA(SUB(at, che), 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not how much debt a firm carries but whether the money funding its accounting build-up comes due before that build-up converts to cash: growth in illiquid operating assets matched dollar-for-dollar by an increase in debt maturing within a year is a funding-maturity mismatch that forces refinancing exactly when accruals are reversing.

The mechanism (asset-liability maturity mismatch) is untested anywhere in the archive, the MIN construction has the best design track record among the accepted signals, and both legs use balance-sheet items so coverage should sit near the archive maximum.

considered.name: SlackErosionWithAccrualBuild
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, ADD(che, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The informative event is not the level of financial slack but its erosion: a firm whose cash position is falling relative to its debt obligations at the same time that its working capital is ballooning is converting liquid resources into soft assets, which is the transition from a comfortable balance sheet into a constrained one.

considered.name: ExternallyBuiltAssetBaseAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), 5), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Five years of cumulative outside capital measures what fraction of the current asset base was built with investors' money rather than retained cash; firms whose balance sheets are structurally externally financed have no demonstrated ability to self-fund, so accrual-heavy earnings today are far more likely to be an accommodation to that dependence than a temporary timing difference.

considered.name: SoftShareOfGrowthEquityFunded
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(ABS(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)))), ABS(DELTA(at, 1))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Two firms can grow their balance sheets identically while one adds plant and the other adds receivables and inventory; what predicts poor returns is the *share* of growth that is soft, and that share is most suspect when the growth was funded by selling equity rather than by retained cash.
considered.reasoning: The flow family's alphas are plausibly absorbed by CMA because their accrual and financing legs both scale with total asset growth; expressing the accrual leg as a bounded share of total balance-sheet growth removes the size-of-growth component and leaves only its composition, which the investment factor does not span. Pairing it with clean-surplus net equity issuance keeps the overvaluation-timing interpretation while using high-coverage balance-sheet items.

considered.name: PeakDebtCapacityAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), TS_MAX(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Debt capacity is firm-specific: what matters is not how levered a firm is versus other firms but whether it has pushed leverage to the highest level it has ever sustained, because that is the point at which lenders stop accommodating and an accrual reversal can no longer be refinanced away.
considered.reasoning: Every leverage conditioner tested so far is a cross-sectional level, which loads on the value and profitability dimensions FF5 already prices; distance from a firm's own five-year maximum leverage is a self-normalized capacity measure that is close to zero for firms at their ceiling regardless of industry or size, so it should be far less spanned by the factor model and more comparable across firms in a pooled regression. This is a genuinely different conditioning concept — proximity to an internal constraint rather than the level of a characteristic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ContractualClaimMixAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Not all liabilities behave alike under stress: interest-bearing debt carries fixed dates and covenants while payables and accrued expenses flex with the business, so a firm whose obligations are predominantly contractual has far less capacity to absorb an accrual reversal than one financed by trade credit at the same total leverage.
considered.reasoning: The archive has repeatedly tested the *amount* of leverage but never its contractual character, and this ratio is deliberately scale-free and independent of total indebtedness, so it should not merely re-proxy the value/leverage tilt that FF5 partially spans. It is built from two universally reported balance-sheet aggregates, so coverage should be at the top of the archive, and it isolates the balance-sheet-pressure channel from the overvaluation channel more cleanly than any quantity-of-financing leg.

considered.name: RaisedCapitalYetCashFell
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), NEG(DELTA(che, 1))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that raised outside capital and still ended the year with less cash consumed the entire raise plus part of its buffer; combined with earnings that are largely accruals, this is direct evidence that the business is burning cash faster than the capital markets are willing to replace it.
considered.reasoning: This is not the previously rejected issuance-minus-cash-change construction, which collapsed by identity into negative operating-plus-investing cash flow; the MIN overlap is positive only when the firm both raised capital *and* depleted cash, so firms that raise and hoard, or that shrink cash while returning capital, sit at neutral rather than loading on the short leg. The overlap operator has the best design record in the archive, and both legs use balance-sheet and clean-surplus items, keeping coverage near 0.10.

considered.name: PayoutEscalationAgainstAccrualDecay
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 4)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), at), 4)))
considered.hypothesis: Capital policy should adjust to fundamentals; when a firm raises its distribution year after year while the cash backing of its earnings deteriorates over the same years, management is either misreading its own business or deliberately signalling a strength that the accounting no longer supports, and that divergence resolves badly.
considered.reasoning: This is not a re-normalization of the archived leverage interaction: it discards the leverage state entirely and instead pairs two fitted multi-year slopes, testing a divergence between the *direction* of accounting quality and the *direction* of payout policy — a concept no archive signal contains, since every payout leg tested has been a contemporaneous level or ratio. The trend construction is what produced the archive's largest alpha, and pairing it with an escalating commitment rather than a static balance-sheet characteristic should give the pooled cross-sectional regression a variable that is not dominated by persistent firm type.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NeverCutDividendFloorAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The binding commitment is not this year's dividend but the floor the firm has never breached in four years: that floor is what management will protect by borrowing, issuing, or deferring investment, so it becomes a genuine claim on future cash precisely when reported earnings stop being cash-backed.
considered.reasoning: Every payout conditioner in the archive measures the current distribution relative to earnings, cash, or assets; the four-year minimum measures the *durable* portion of the commitment, which distinguishes a firm with a large sustained dividend from one that just paid a large special or recently initiated, and treats an unreported dividend as zero, which is the economically correct convention. It replaces the rejected three-leg industry neutralization with a two-leg structure that has historically preserved Fama-MacBeth slope power, while targeting the rigidity mechanism that generated the archive's largest alphas.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RigidityAmplifiedAccrualMagnitude
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Claim rigidity does not create mispricing, it amplifies it symmetrically: among firms with mostly contractual obligations, aggressive accruals are punished harder and genuinely cash-backed earnings are rewarded more, because these are the firms for which the difference between paper profit and cash actually determines solvency.
considered.reasoning: Every rigid-claim signal in the archive compresses accruals into a rank, discarding magnitude, which is precisely what the strongest cross-sectional slopes (DollarBloat fmb −4.01, SoftFundingIntensity −3.61) retain — so this tests whether keeping signed accrual magnitude while letting rigidity scale it can deliver the FMB slope that the rank-product family loses. Unlike the gen-4 proposal rejected for symmetric amplification, the hypothesis here is explicitly two-sided and matches the constrained-firm amplification story, so the functional form and the economics agree.

considered.name: BookTaxGapUnderRigidClaims
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(txp, 0), 1), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings that generate no incremental tax obligation are the least likely to be real, and the firms least able to survive that discovery are those whose obligations are contractual rather than operating, so the two diagnostics should reinforce each other.
considered.reasoning: The book-tax accrual leg owns the archive's best Sharpe (−0.49) together with a strong slope (fmb −3.56), and the contractual-claim conditioner owns one of its largest alphas (−5.8%, t −3.82), and these are the two ingredients that have never been paired; because the tax-based accrual measure is a sharper earnings-quality signal than the raw accrual it should carry more cross-sectional slope into the interaction than ib − oancf did. With two generations remaining this is a deliberate consolidation test of the archive's two best-performing components rather than an exploratory swap.

considered.name: NearTermCashCallsVersusCash
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dlc, TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4)), ADD(che, ADD(dlc, TS_MIN(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 4))))))
considered.hypothesis: The binding constraint is the cash the firm must produce within twelve months — debt maturing this year plus the dividend it has never cut — measured against the cash it actually holds; when those claims dominate the liquidity available and reported earnings are mostly accruals, the required cash simply is not there.
considered.reasoning: The rejected version buried a sub-1%-of-assets dividend floor inside total debt, where it was numerically irrelevant; restricting the numerator to claims due within the year makes the two components comparable in magnitude (short-term debt and annual dividends are both typically low-single-digit percentages of assets) so the dividend rigidity genuinely contributes. The conditioner is bounded in [0,1], shares no variable with the accrual leg, and is a liquidity-coverage concept rather than the capital-structure-composition ratio already tested.

considered.name: DividendRaisedOnBorrowedMoney
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), DELTA(COALESCE(dvc, 0), 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Increasing the dividend is a public commitment to future cash payments; doing so in the same year the firm takes in net outside capital means the commitment is being escalated on borrowed strength, and if the earnings behind it are accrual-based the escalation is a signalling gamble rather than a statement of capacity.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the problematic cushion denominator — which could be near zero or negative for exactly the distressed firms it targeted — in favour of an overlap of two flows, the construction with the best design record in this archive, so no division by a possibly-negative capacity is involved. It is also a different economic event from anything tested: the archive's payout legs are all levels or floors, whereas this isolates the *act of raising* the dividend while simultaneously raising capital.

considered.name: CapitalRaisedWhileFixedAssetsShrank
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), NEG(DELTA(SUB(at, act), 1))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm raises outside capital in a year its long-lived asset base is shrinking, the money did not fund investment — it was absorbed by the operating cycle or by losses — and that is the least productive possible use of external finance, especially when reported profit is accrual-driven.
considered.reasoning: The previous version failed to resolve the double-count because Δche and Δdlc appeared in both legs; replacing the cash-drawdown leg with the decline in non-current assets removes every shared term with the accrual leg while preserving the "the raise was consumed, not invested" economics. considered.name: DebtVersusServicingResourcesAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(che, MAX(ADD(ib, dp), dp))))))
considered.hypothesis: Debt should be judged against the resources available to service it — cash on hand plus a year of pre-depreciation earnings — and a firm whose obligations dwarf those resources cannot absorb an accrual reversal, because the reversal removes precisely the reported profit that the servicing capacity was assumed to contain.
considered.reasoning: The rejected version put oancf in both legs, making the product close to a squared low-cash-flow characteristic; this conditioner contains no oancf at all, and while ib appears in both, it enters with opposing effects (higher earnings raise the accrual leg but also raise servicing capacity, lowering the conditioner), so the interaction cannot be a same-direction double count. considered.name: BoundedAccrualShareFinanced
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), ABS(oancf)))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is the fraction of reported profit that is not backed by cash, not its size relative to assets: a firm whose entire earnings figure is accrual while its cash flow is negative is qualitatively different from an asset-heavy firm with the same accrual-to-assets ratio, and that qualitative difference is what external funding exposes.
considered.reasoning: Every accrual leg in this archive is deflated by assets, which makes it mechanically correlated with asset intensity and heavily outlier-driven; a bounded accrual-share-of-earnings measure in [−1, 1] is a different economic construct — earnings composition rather than balance-sheet intensity — and its boundedness should produce more monotone cross-sectional behaviour without the winsorization crutch. considered.name: DividendsAbsorbingOperatingCash
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(oancf), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The economically correct test of distribution sustainability is what share of the cash the business actually generates is consumed by the dividend; a firm handing most of its operating cash to shareholders while simultaneously taking capital in from them is running a distribution policy that operations do not support.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested payout strain against reported earnings (|ib|) and against cash holdings (che), and both produced the run's best joint evidence, but never against operating cash flow — the one denominator that directly measures the firm's ability to fund the payout, and the one that makes the strain leg itself an accruals-theme construct rather than a balance-sheet characteristic. considered.name: DeterioratingCashCallCoverageBloat
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dlc, COALESCE(dvc, 0)), ADD(che, ADD(dlc, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What predicts trouble is not a firm's standing liquidity profile — which the market has long since priced as a firm type — but a deterioration in it: obligations coming due within the year rising relative to cash on hand, in the same year working capital balloons, marks the transition into a funding squeeze.

considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dvt, COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Preferred dividends are a claim that ranks ahead of common shareholders and must be served before any residual value accrues to them; when the earnings supporting that seniority structure are accrual-based rather than cash, the common equity is the tranche that absorbs the shortfall.
considered.reasoning: Claim *seniority* is the one financing dimension this archive has never touched — every conditioner so far has measured quantity, maturity, composition or rigidity of claims, but none their priority — and the total-minus-common dividend difference isolates it using a reported item (dvt) that no prior signal has used. considered.name: TradeCreditWithdrawalReplacedByMarkets
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Suppliers monitor their customers more closely than public investors do; when operating liabilities shrink while the firm simultaneously raises capital from markets, informed trade creditors are withdrawing and being replaced by uninformed outside capital.

considered.name: PositivePartBorrowedDividends
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(MIN(MUL(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), INDICATOR(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), 0)), COALESCE(dvc, 0)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Borrowing to fund a dividend is a specific, one-sided event: it requires debt to actually increase and cash to actually go out, so the measure should be the overlap of the *positive part* of the debt change with the dividend, not a minimum that silently turns into a debt-paydown measure whenever borrowings fall.
considered.reasoning: The archived DebtCoveredDividendsSoftEarnings (alpha −1.8%, fmb −1.20) was mismeasured exactly as the critique of my previous proposal describes — when the debt change was negative its MIN returned the paydown amount, placing disciplined deleveraging payers in the same tail as accrual-heavy borrowers — and using INDICATOR to take the positive part repairs that without changing any other component. Only one thing changes relative to the archived signal, so attribution is clean, and if the repaired overlap strengthens both statistics it validates the round-trip mechanism that has run through this entire archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierRetreatWhileShareholdersPaid
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(oancf), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))))
considered.hypothesis: Trade creditors are the best-informed monitors a firm has; when they are pulling back operating credit while management continues to route most of the firm's operating cash to shareholders, the firm is prioritizing the junior claimants over the very financiers who see its cash cycle up close.
considered.reasoning: This joins the two strongest new slopes produced this run — supplier-credit withdrawal (fmb −2.77 at 0.112 coverage) and dividends as a share of operating cash (fmb −4.43) — and unlike the recombinations rejected earlier the legs come from different information sources (balance-sheet operating liabilities versus payout policy against cash flow) and share no variable. The resulting state is economically vivid and one no archive signal captures: informed creditors exiting while distributions continue.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutCoverageDeteriorationFunded
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(oancf), COALESCE(dvc, 0))), 1)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The informative event is the year in which the dividend's claim on operating cash jumps — because cash flow fell, the payout rose, or both — and the firm meets the resulting gap by raising outside capital rather than by cutting the distribution.
considered.reasoning: The level version of this coverage ratio produced the archive's best slope but only a −2.5% alpha at t −1.89, the signature of a variable that identifies firm type as much as change in condition; differencing it isolates the deterioration event, the same modification that lifted the cash-call conditioner from a null slope to a reliable −3.3% alpha at t −3.69 in gen 8. It preserves the two-leg structure and keeps the financing leg that makes the interaction an accruals-times-financing statement rather than a payout characteristic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CreditWithdrawalAndTighteningCashCalls
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dlc, COALESCE(dvc, 0)), ADD(che, ADD(dlc, COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Two independent monitors tightening at once — suppliers shortening terms and the twelve-month cash calendar growing relative to available cash — describe a firm whose funding is contracting from both the operating and the financial side while its obligations are rising.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are dynamic rather than static, both come from gen-8 mechanisms that worked (supplier retreat: fmb −2.77, alpha −2.2%; deteriorating cash-call coverage: alpha −3.3%, t −3.69), and both are computed from universally reported balance-sheet items, so this should be the highest-coverage proposal in the batch at roughly 0.112. It is the natural high-coverage consolidation to close the run: a pure squeeze signal with no static distress characteristic that could carry the result through a factor-loading mismatch rather than a genuine interaction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DistributionCoverageDecayWithSoftEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), ABS(oancf)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, ADD(ABS(oancf), dvt)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: When the share of a firm's operating cash claimed by total distributions — common and preferred together — rises while a growing fraction of reported profit is non-cash, the firm is committing more cash to claimholders exactly as its ability to generate that cash deteriorates.
considered.reasoning: The rejected version failed because a non-negative preferred-claim level puts the large block of non-preferred firms at the bottom of the rank rather than the middle; taking the *change* in total distribution coverage fixes this structurally, since firms with no distributions have a change of exactly zero, which sits at the centre of a two-sided distribution rather than at an extreme. Both legs are now continuous and bounded — the accrual share in [−1,1] and the coverage change symmetric around zero — and neither is a static distress characteristic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TradeCreditReplacedByContractualDebt
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), at))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), ADD(ceq, ADD(dltt, dlc))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: When suppliers shorten terms, the firm must replace flexible, interest-free operating credit with contractual borrowing; that substitution converts a claim that bends in bad times into one that does not, and it is initiated by the creditors who monitor the firm most closely.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the heavy-zero-mass borrowed-dividend overlap (fmb −0.86) with a continuous, symmetric leverage-share *change*, so both legs of the product are two-sided and free of tied blocks, addressing the effective-sample objection directly. The economics are also tighter than the earlier pairing: it is the literal substitution of informed trade credit by contractual debt within a single year, using only high-coverage balance-sheet items so coverage should stay near the archive maximum of 0.112.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutCoverageWithHardeningClaims
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dvc, 0), ADD(ABS(oancf), COALESCE(dvc, 0)))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A dividend that already consumes most of operating cash becomes dangerous when the firm's obligation mix is hardening — flexible operating liabilities giving way to contractual debt — because each year less of the balance sheet can absorb a cash shortfall without a covenant or a maturity forcing the issue.
considered.reasoning: The critique of the static debt-share conditioner is well founded — it has produced large alphas with null slopes in four separate archive signals, the signature of a persistent distress characteristic mis-loading against FF5 — so this replaces the level with its one-year change, which identifies firms whose claim structure is *becoming* rigid rather than firms that are permanently levered. Paired with the archive's strongest cross-sectional leg (payout absorption of operating cash, fmb −4.43), both components now vary within firm over time, which is the configuration that has consistently produced joint slope and alpha evidence in this run.

critic_notes.rationale: The rank product is internally coherent and correctly implements the "accruals only bite among net issuers" conditioning, but it sits very close to the published joint accruals/net-external-financing evidence (Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan), so it is best treated as a baseline rather than a discovery.

A 0-5 integer count produces massive ties and coarse portfolio sorts, the joint-indicator event (~25% per year unconditionally) makes the extreme bucket small and unstable, and the five-year window cuts coverage, so the persistence idea — itself close to known accrual-persistence work — is unlikely to be testable in this form.

SUMRANK of accrual change and debt growth is a plain equal-weight composite of two independently documented predictors (change-in-accruals and debt issuance/asset growth) with no conditioning or new economic content, so it adds little beyond either component.

The hypothesis is explicitly conditional ("high accruals at firms returning cash are far less suspicious") but the expression is an additive rank difference that applies an identical accrual penalty at every payout level, so the stated mechanism is not what the formula computes; it also largely reassembles the known accrual and payout-yield anomalies.

The conditional rank-product structure is sound and the balance-sheet accrual construction is defensible, but GROWTH(csho) is unadjusted for splits and stock dividends, so the "financing" leg is heavily contaminated by non-economic share-count changes and is not a clean proxy for the (already published) share-issuance anomaly.

Summing accrual and net-financing dollars before scaling is a legitimate, magnitude-preserving commensurate combination with high coverage, though it is largely a linear re-expression of the same accruals-plus-external-financing composite as the first proposal and will be dominated by whichever component has larger cross-sectional variance.

The clean-surplus reconstruction of net external capital is a substantive, coverage-motivated fix to the gen-0 winner's binding constraint and is internally consistent, though it inherits exposure to the well-known net-external-financing anomaly and Δceq is contaminated by OCI and non-issuance equity movements.
This is a single-knob normalization tweak of the gen-0 winner that leaves both legs and the ~10% coverage bottleneck untouched, making it a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism.

Decomposing net financing into an equity-versus-debt tilt is an economically informative test of the market-timing versus balance-sheet-pressure channel, but the leg mechanically assigns high (bad) scores to firms merely repaying debt, which pushes against the usual positive return signal from debt retirement and muddies the sign interpretation.

By the cash-flow identity, issuance minus Δcash is approximately −(CFO + CFI), so the second leg rises whenever operating cash flow falls — the same thing the first leg (ib − oancf) already measures — making this a partially redundant double-count of low CFO and heavy capex rather than the claimed "liquidity destination" interaction.

The hard gate plus preserved winsorized magnitude is internally coherent and cleanly isolates whether the payoff comes from gating or from accrual size, though it is a mechanical restatement of the same two ingredients and still inherits the low coverage of the cash-flow issuance items.

The stock-versus-multi-year-financing contrast is a genuine reformulation rather than a smoothing tweak, but the non-cash working capital level leg is close to the published net-operating-assets/balance-sheet-bloat anomaly and is highly industry-persistent, so the long-short spread risks being a sector bet absent industry neutralization.

Swapping the archive's dividend indicator for a payout-intensity rank is a near-cosmetic softening of BorrowedDistributionsWithSoftEarnings — RANK of a variable with a ~50% point mass at zero still lumps all non-payers at one degenerate rank, so the "continuous support" argument is largely illusory — and the added leg is essentially dividend yield, a known standalone predictor whose usual positive return relation fights the stated negative sign.

The conditioning leg dvc/at − ib/at is dominated by −ROA rather than by payout excess (loss-making non-payers, not over-distributing payers, load highest), so the expression contradicts the stated hypothesis and mostly rediscovers the profitability effect, while also double-counting ib against the accrual leg.

RANK(LOG(at)) is a monotone transform of RANK(at), so this is simply a size tilt bolted onto an existing rank product — mechanically it makes the extreme portfolios a size sort, its premise contradicts the well-documented finding that accrual and issuance mispricing is concentrated in small, hard-to-arbitrage firms, and "reduces microcap noise" is a portfolio-engineering rationale rather than an economic mechanism.

Introducing an accounting-quality dimension not yet used in the archive is worthwhile, but Δtxp is a weak proxy for the book-tax gap (the published Hanlon/Lev-Nissim anomaly uses imputed taxable income) and is itself a standard component of the Sloan accrual definition, so the leg partly refines rather than genuinely diversifies the accrual measure, and COALESCE-to-zero on a sparsely reported item risks conflating non-reporting with zero tax accrual.

The MIN overlap is a genuinely well-constructed formalization of "borrowing to pay the dividend" — it is positive only when both flows are jointly positive, correctly parks self-funded payers and investment-driven borrowers near neutral, and uses high-coverage items — making it a substantively different construction rather than a re-weighting of the archived gate.

Testing the transition into external dependence rather than its level is a legitimate and previously untried timing question, though taking a difference of an already-differenced balance-sheet flow doubles the measurement noise and risks producing a mechanical one-year reversal rather than the claimed underreaction.

This is PayoutStrainExternallyFunded with the accrual leg swapped for the archive's BookTaxGapFinancedGrowth accrual leg — a mechanical recombination of two already-tested triples rather than a new mechanism, and the third rank multiplication further dilutes an already thin (0.084) sample.

Identically a cosmetic swap: CleanSurplusFundedWCBloat multiplied by the same payout-strain rank already tested in PayoutStrainExternallyFunded, so the only genuinely new information is a coverage difference, which does not justify a generation.

The debt-maturity-composition leg is a genuinely distinct financing-pressure channel (no quantity-of-capital-raised leg in the archive captures it), the expression matches the hypothesis and the sign direction is unambiguous, and coverage should be high; the main residual risk is that short-term debt share shifts partly reflect firm size/credit quality rather than rollover strain.

The long-lived-asset side of accounting quality is a legitimate gap in the archive (and DEPI-style depreciation-rate declines are a recognized manipulation flag), but Δ(dp/at) falls mechanically when the asset base grows fast, which is exactly what the externally-financed-growth leg measures, so the interaction is largely asset-growth squared and any result will not identify the stated expense-recognition mechanism.

The `ib` terms cancel algebraically — the bracket reduces to (Δdebt + Δceq + dvc − oancf)/at — so despite the hypothesis the signal contains no accrual/earnings-quality content at all, and dvc enters both the level and the strain weight, double-counting the payout term.

Decomposing the netted working-capital accrual into asset-build and payable-stretch sides is a substantive re-specification rather than a re-weighting and the expression matches the hypothesis, but the liability leg bets against the documented direction of the accrual anomaly (payables growth lowers accruals and predicts higher returns) on thin justification, and the three-way rank product will diffuse whatever spread survives.

A coherent and internally consistent generalization of the two archived overlap signals (debt→dividends and equity→dividends) that broadens both the source and use legs, but it is an incremental union of already-tested components and inherits the ~8% coverage penalty of prstkc, so the upside is a modest sharpening rather than a new mechanism.

This is an operator swap on the immediately preceding proposal with identical ingredients, and because an additive rank lets the accrual leg alone drive the extremes, the signal collapses substantially toward the plain Sloan accrual anomaly — a methodological diagnostic dressed up as an economic hypothesis.

The expression multiplies a *signed* winsorized dollar-bloat ratio by a strictly positive strain rank, so payout strain amplifies both tails symmetrically — implying self-funded firms with rigid dividends are the strongest buys — which does not match the stated one-sided "forced write-off" mechanism, and the construction otherwise overlaps heavily with the already-tested PayoutStrainExternallyFunded.

The financial-slack stock is a genuinely untested conditioning dimension in this archive and the level-variable argument for a better FMB slope is sensible, but (lt−che)/at is close to a plain book-leverage characteristic with its own known return relation, and a third multiplicative rank leg risks further diluting the spread as it did in earlier triple products.

Replacing the differenced maturity leg with its persistent level is a defensible single-variable diagnostic on an archive signal that showed alpha without a slope, though it sits close to being a level-versus-change restatement and both legs (accruals, short-term debt share) are individually documented characteristics.

This is the best-motivated proposal in the batch: the MIN overlap is correctly constructed (prstkc is non-negative, deleveraging repurchasers and investment-driven borrowers stay neutral), and because the buyback literature carries the opposite prior it is a real discrimination test between "capital recycling per se" and "dividend rigidity" rather than a restatement — the main caveat being low prstkc coverage.

This is a near-duplicate of NoSlackExternallyFundedAccruals whose only substantive change is swapping one highly correlated leverage-slack proxy for another, since the outer RANK is a monotone transform that by the proposer's own admission leaves the portfolio sort identical — so the entire claimed gain rests on a rescaling of the FMB regressor rather than new economics.

This is a mechanical rank-average of two already-tested archive constructs (ExternallyMatchedBloatDollars and an accrual×net-debt state interaction) rather than a new mechanism, and the additive SUMRANK contradicts the stated "both most of all" conjunctive logic while making the result an ensemble whose metrics will largely interpolate the parents'.

A defensible, internally consistent tightening of the failed ShortTermDebtRelianceSoftEarnings conditioner into a bounded cash-coverage-of-maturing-debt ratio, though it remains close to the well-documented "accruals are stronger among financially constrained firms" result and risks proxying for low cash holdings rather than genuine rollover strain.

The substitution of a cash-based for an earnings-based payout-strain denominator is a legitimate and diagnostic change relative to PayoutStrainExternallyFunded, but dvc/(che+dvc) is largely an inverse-cash-holdings characteristic that overlaps the slack conditioner already tested, and the triple rank product will continue to squash cross-sectional slope power.

The fitted multi-year accrual trend is a genuinely different statistical object from the levels, one-year changes, volatilities and TS_RANKs already tried, and the sign logic is coherent, though a 4-year OLS slope on a noisy ratio may be mostly estimation error and the net-debt leg re-treads ground the archive has repeatedly explored.

The two legs are not conceptually separate as claimed — by the balance-sheet identity Δ(at−che)−Δ(lt−debt) equals Δceq+Δdebt−Δche, which differs from the financing leg only by retained earnings minus the cash change — so the expression is close to a squared financing variable, and the accrual leg itself is a direct restatement of the published net-operating-assets/NOA-growth anomaly.

This is a single-operator (RANK→IND_RANK) perturbation of the archived AccrualQualityDriftUnderLeverage rather than a substantively different construction, and its motivating diagnosis is economically shaky — persistent industry composition would show up *in* the Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional slope rather than "averaging out" of it, so the claim that sector-neutralizing will convert alpha into a pooled slope is unsupported.

Recasting the accrual leg as a bounded soft-share-of-total-growth is a real construction change (not just a rescaling) with a defensible CMA-orthogonalization motive, though it remains inside the heavily mined bloat×equity-issuance family whose best archive member (WorkingCapitalBloatEquityFunded) it must beat, and the ABS-sum denominator will be noisy for firms with near-zero asset growth.

Distance-from-own-leverage-peak is a genuinely new, self-normalized conditioning concept that is internally consistent (the SUB is weakly negative, so the high-rank/high-accrual corner is the at-capacity corner as the hypothesis requires), with the main testable risk being a large point mass of ties at zero for firms whose leverage is currently at its five-year high.

Applying IND_RANK to all three legs of PayoutStrainExternallyFunded is a mechanical neutralization of an existing archive signal with no change to the economics, exactly the kind of cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and the FF5 alpha it seeks to protect is more likely diluted by the dividend-payer profitability tilt than by raw sector membership.

Debt-share-of-total-liabilities is a legitimately untested conditioner in this archive and is scale-free with high coverage, but the design is thin — a two-term rank product on top of the classic accrual anomaly — so its incremental value rests entirely on whether claim *composition* conditions accrual mispricing differently from the leverage *levels* already tested and mostly failed.

The MIN overlap does avoid the degenerate issuance-minus-cash-change identity and the sign logic is coherent, but the two legs are mechanically linked through oancf (low operating cash simultaneously raises measured accruals and drives the cash decline), so the "interaction" risks being a double-count of a single cash-burn construct; also the debt leg inconsistently drops dlc relative to the rest of the archive.

Adding a four-year dividend floor (typically well under 1% of assets) to total debt inside a single ratio is numerically negligible — the conditioner is >95% driven by debt/(lt+ceq) — so this is effectively a re-run of the archive's ContractualClaimMixAccruals with a cosmetically different denominator, and it inherits that family's near-zero FMB slope with an alpha that likely comes from the leverage leg alone rather than any interaction.

The form is internally consistent (a strictly positive rank multiplier scales signed accrual magnitude, matching the stated two-sided amplification story) and the rank-vs-magnitude encoding question is a legitimate diagnostic for the run's FMB/alpha divergence, but it remains a functional-form variant of ContractualClaimMixAccruals whose ordering will be dominated by accrual outliers even after 1% winsorization, so the upside is modest.

The denominator (che + ceq) can be near zero or negative for exactly the distressed, market-dependent firms the hypothesis targets, which flips the ratio's sign and dumps genuinely dependent firms into the wrong tail; the inner WINSOR is also redundant under an outer RANK, and the construct is otherwise the archive's well-worn accrual × external-financing template with a new scaler.

The claimed "cleaning" is incomplete — removing oancf simply substitutes a new shared term, since DELTA(che) enters the bloat leg (with a negative sign) and the burn leg (as NEG(DELTA(che))) so a cash drawdown mechanically raises both legs, and DELTA(dlc) likewise appears in both — meaning the double-counting objection that motivated the revision is not actually resolved.

oancf drives both legs (low operating cash flow simultaneously raises ib − oancf and the debt/cash-flow multiple), so the product is largely a squared low-cash-flow characteristic rather than an accrual × leverage interaction; the MAX(oancf, dp) floor is also undefined when dp is zero or missing and produces explosive ratios for near-zero denominators.

This is a genuinely untested pairing of two independently motivated legs with clean, non-overlapping inputs and a coherent negative sign, but the proposal ignores the strong archive pattern that every "rigid claim" conditioner delivers roughly the same −5% alpha with a near-zero FMB slope regardless of which earnings-quality leg it multiplies, so it should be run alongside the conditioner standalone to establish that any interaction exists at all.

This is PayoutStrainExternallyFunded with the accrual leg swapped for the already-tested book-tax leg — a cosmetic recombination of two archived signals whose legs are highly collinear (both are ib−oancf-driven), and the triple rank product further dilutes the cross-sectional slope rather than testing a new mechanism.

A defensible flow-versus-state additivity test, but it is a mechanical triple product of two fully archived signals whose conditioner (NearTermCashCallsVersusCash) carried a near-zero FMB slope (−0.26) with a large alpha that most plausibly reflects a leverage/distress factor mismatch rather than a priceable interaction, so the combination is likely to inherit the null slope while diluting the bloat leg.

The two-leg overlap-plus-capacity construction is cleaner than the triple product and the stated contrast with the previous proposal is a legitimate design experiment, but it remains a straight product of two already-evaluated components and is nearly a duplicate of the proposal immediately preceding it, so at most one of the two deserves a slot.

Re-encoding accruals as a bounded share of earnings-plus-cash-flow is a genuinely different economic construct (earnings composition rather than balance-sheet intensity) rather than a cosmetic variant, though the stated outlier motivation is weak since the subsequent RANK already neutralizes tail influence — the real claim being tested is the change in cross-sectional ordering, which is worth testing against CleanSurplusFundedWCBloat.

This is the archived NearTermCashCallsVersusCash with only the accrual deflator changed, and since that signal's near-zero FMB almost certainly comes from the static liquidity/leverage state leg rather than from accrual outliers, the proposed diagnostic is unlikely to identify what its reasoning claims it will.

It changes two things at once relative to the weak archived DebtCoveredDividendsSoftEarnings (accrual encoding and deflator), making attribution impossible, and the construction is unsound — MIN(Δdebt, dvc) is not a round-trip overlap when Δdebt is negative (it then measures debt paydown), and the denominator che+dvc is not strictly positive by construction as claimed, so near-zero-cash firms will produce explosive values on both signs.

This is a one-denominator rescale of the archived SeniorClaimsAheadOfAccruals rather than a new mechanism, and the stated justification is internally inconsistent — a non-negative preferred-claim ratio puts the (large) zero mass of non-preferred firms at the *bottom* of the rank, not "in the neutral middle," so the interaction is effectively driven by a small, persistent subset of preferred-issuing firms whose ratio explodes whenever cash is near zero.

It is a rank-product recombination of two already-tested legs rather than a new mechanism, but the legs share no variable, come from genuinely different information sources (operating-liability dynamics vs. payout-to-cash-flow), and the "informed creditors exiting while distributions continue" state is not captured elsewhere in the archive — though note the ABS(oancf) denominator makes cash-flow-negative payers score high, which is a different economics than "most of operating cash paid out."

Another two-archive-leg product, and the chosen partner leg (positive-part borrowed dividends, fmb −0.86) has both a null cross-sectional slope and a very heavy zero mass, so multiplying it by ranks will produce large tied blocks and an effective sample close to the archived signal it derives from — low expected incremental information relative to proposal #2.

The debt/total-liabilities conditioner has repeatedly delivered large FF5 alphas with near-zero Fama-MacBeth slopes across the archive (ContractualClaimMixAccruals, BookTaxGapUnderRigidClaims, NearTermCashCalls, DebtVersusServicingResources), which is the signature of a static leverage/distress characteristic mis-loading against FF5 rather than a real interaction; pairing it with a second static payout characteristic makes that diagnosis more likely, not less.

Differencing the payout-coverage ratio is a substantive (not cosmetic) response to the level version's type-vs-event ambiguity and the financing leg keeps the cross-theme structure, but the reasoning misdescribes the result as "an accruals-times-financing statement" when no accrual term appears, and the change leg is identically zero for all non-payers, which will concentrate the variation in a minority of firms.

Both legs are changes rather than levels, which is the right way to test whether the run's alphas survive removal of static distress characteristics, and coverage should be high; the main reservation is that it is again a recombination of two previously tested legs and the delta of a bounded liquidity ratio is likely to be noisy enough to dilute the already-modest single-leg slopes.
